setup: In April 1644 the Ming dynasty — the last ethnically Chinese house to rule a unified China — collapses, and not at the hands of foreigners: a peasant rebel named Li Zicheng takes Beijing and the last Ming emperor hangs himself behind the palace. Into that vacuum walks a people almost nobody outside the northeast had been watching. They are the Jurchens, a Tungusic forest-and-river people from Manchuria, fur-trappers and horse-raiders, nominal Ming tributaries who number perhaps a million souls. One chieftain has spent thirty years welding their rival clans into a single war-machine, and his heirs have given themselves a new name — Manchu — and a new dynasty claiming the Mandate of Heaven: the Qing. What is at stake here is the most lopsided arithmetic in history. A million conquerors are about to take, and then hold, a country of over a hundred million — and the question of how a tiny outside elite makes that stick runs under all 268 years that follow.

bridge: Chapter 1 left the Manchus inside the wall and on the throne in Beijing, having taken the capital in 1644 and ground down the southern Ming loyalists over the next two decades. They held China by a careful machine: a dual government pairing every senior Manchu with a Han Chinese deputy, banner garrisons walled into Chinese cities, and the queue order branded on every man's scalp as a daily badge of submission. But the dynasty had a soft spot the conquest never solved — its emperors kept dying young of smallpox, and in 1661 the throne passes to a seven-year-old boy. The whole apparatus is intact; whether a child can grow into it is the open question.
setup: That boy takes the reign name Kangxi, and he will hold the throne for sixty-one years — the longest reign in Chinese history and, by most reckonings, one of the two or three greatest. But he inherits a regency dominated by a Manchu strongman, an empire whose southern third is run by three semi-independent Chinese warlords, an unfinished conquest with Taiwan still in rebel hands, and frontiers pressing in from Russia and the Mongol steppe. This is the chapter where the empire grows into its adult shape: a teenage emperor seizing personal power, surviving a civil war that nearly tore the south away, signing China's first treaty with a European power as equals, and riding out onto the steppe himself to fight the last great nomad empire. It is also where a remarkable cross-cultural experiment with the Jesuits opens — and where it sours.

bridge: Kangxi's sixty-one years (Chapter 2) conquered the south, annexed Taiwan, fixed the Russian border, and broke the Mongol warlord Galdan — but his one great failure was his own children. He had too many sons, kept naming and unnaming an heir, and left the succession a poisoned brawl. He also made a generous, popular, and fiscally dangerous promise late in life: he froze the head-tax total forever. When he dies in 1722, his fourth son takes the throne amid never-silenced rumors that he faked the will. The conquest is long secure; what is unsettled is whether the machine that runs it can be made to work without a genius personally driving it every day.
setup: That fourth son reigns as Yongzheng for only thirteen years, he is the least famous of the three High Qing emperors, and he may be the most important. If Kangxi conquered and his own son Qianlong would display, Yongzheng built the machine. A workaholic autocrat said to sleep four hours a night, he redesigns how China is governed: a secret-memorial channel that gives the throne its own spy network, and a small inner cabinet — the Grand Council — that quietly displaces the slow formal bureaucracy and concentrates power in the emperor's person more tightly than almost any other early modern state. He also does the unglamorous work an empire runs on — a serious anti-corruption pay reform, a quietly progressive shift of taxes off bodies and onto land — and reveals, in his strange public argument with a treason suspect, the deepest nerve of the whole dynasty: a conquest elite still anxiously arguing for its own right to rule.

bridge: Across the last two chapters the Qing went from conquest to consolidation: Kangxi grew the empire and Yongzheng (Chapter 3) rebuilt its machinery — the Grand Council, the secret memorials, a cleaned-up fiscal system — concentrating power in the throne and leaving a full treasury. In 1735 that throne passes smoothly, for once, to Yongzheng's son. He inherits the most powerful state on Earth, the engine tuned and the coffers full. The reign that follows is the summit. It is also, in hindsight, where the rot quietly sets in — which is exactly why the high point and the beginning of the fall turn out to be the same fifty years.
setup: He reigns as Qianlong for sixty years, then rules three more from behind a screen, deliberately stopping one year short of his grandfather's record. Under him the Qing is unambiguously the largest, richest, and most populous empire in the world, its share of the global economy perhaps a quarter to a third — larger than all of Europe combined. His armies finish the seventy-year war with the Dzungars in an extermination historians now describe, with the term flagged as anachronistic, as genocide, and conquer the vast new region named Xinjiang, roughly doubling the empire and drawing the borders the People's Republic claims today. His scholars assemble the largest book collection in human history — and burn or mutilate thousands of works in the censorship sweep that runs alongside it. And in old age he hands the state to a beautiful, monumentally corrupt favorite while a British embassy arrives asking, in effect, whether China understands what is coming. It does not.

bridge: The last four chapters followed the politics — the conquest, then the long imperial summit under Kangxi, Yongzheng, and Qianlong, ending with a British embassy turned away in 1793 by an emperor who saw no reason China should want anything Europe made. From inside the Qing that confidence was entirely rational: China genuinely was the largest economy on Earth. This chapter steps out of the story of emperors and campaigns to explain why — because the thing that made the High Qing the center of the world is exactly the thing whose collapse in the next century is so total.
setup: For roughly two centuries, from about 1680 to 1820, the Qing sat at the hub of the early global economy. The world wanted three things only China made well — tea, silk, and porcelain — and paid for them in silver, so a huge share of all the silver dug out of the Americas flowed across the oceans and into China, which collected the receipts. Europe's merchants were funneled through a single port, Canton, dealing only with a licensed guild, on terms China dictated. Underneath the silver, a demographic event with no precedent: New World crops let the population roughly triple past 300 million, close to a third of all humans alive. It looks permanent and unshakeable. But the same chapter quietly assembles the trap — a frozen tax base, too many people on too little land, and a trade imbalance that is a loaded gun waiting for the commodity that will finally reverse the silver's direction.

bridge: Chapter 5 stepped out of the chronology to show the machine underneath the High Qing: a world economy pumping American silver into China for its tea and porcelain, a population tripled past 300 million by New World crops, and — hidden in the prosperity — a frozen tax base, land hunger, and a trade imbalance the British could not pay for in silver forever. That was the system at its summit. This chapter is the year the luck runs out: a peasant revolt breaks out in 1796, the very year Qianlong formally steps down, as if the dynasty's fortune retired with him.
setup: The White Lotus Rebellion — a millenarian folk-Buddhist uprising among the landless migrants the last chapter created — takes eight years and a fortune to crush, and the crushing exposes everything the dynasty had been hiding from itself: the once-terrifying Eight Banners are now a pampered, drilled-for-show, opium-smoking caste who cannot campaign, the war is won by corruption-riddled local militias, and the treasury Qianlong inherited is gone. Then the loaded gun of Chapter 5 goes off. To reverse the silver flow, the British find one commodity China will buy without limit: opium, grown in India and smuggled in through Canton. The drug breeds mass addiction and drains silver back out so fast that ordinary peasants' real taxes quietly double. By the late 1830s the emperor must choose between legalizing the drug and crushing it — and he picks the most formidable, incorruptible official in the empire to crush it.

bridge: Chapter 6 ended with the dynasty's rot exposed and the silver crisis at a head: opium smuggled in through Canton was draining the silver that two centuries of tea exports had pulled in, breeding mass addiction and quietly doubling the peasants' tax burden. The Daoguang Emperor chose total suppression and sent his most formidable, incorruptible official, Lin Zexu, to Canton with full powers to end the trade. Lin was about to do his job perfectly. He was also about to be perfectly wrong about what would follow — the hinge this whole chapter turns on.
setup: In 1839 Lin Zexu blockades the foreign merchants, seizes roughly a thousand tons of opium, and destroys it. By the moral logic of the Qing state it is a clean victory — an honest official enforcing China's own law inside China's own borders. By the logic of the industrial world now arriving, he has handed Britain the pretext it wanted. The First Opium War is one of the most morally lopsided wars in modern history — Britain fighting to force a destructive narcotic on China and calling it free trade — and one of the most militarily lopsided, because the technological gap Qianlong never grasped turns out to be total, symbolized by a single iron, steam-powered gunboat that can sail up China's rivers and shatter wooden war junks that cannot reply. The treaty that ends it becomes the template for a century: ceded Hong Kong, opened ports, an indemnity, and the corrosive legal privileges that Chinese nationalism will later brand the "unequal treaties."

bridge: Two long pressures have been building. Chapter 6 showed the dynasty's armies rotted into helplessness and a squeezed, land-hungry peasantry radicalized by the silver drain. Chapter 7 showed the Qing's claim to be the world's center publicly shattered by the First Opium War and the unequal treaties that followed. Now those two crises — internal collapse and external humiliation — converge, and the result is the bloodiest civil war in human history before the twentieth century, a war that kills somewhere between 20 and 30 million people. The honest framing is that we do not know within ten million, which itself tells you the scale.
setup: It begins with a man who failed the civil service exam four times, fell into a fevered illness, and emerged convinced he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ, sent to destroy demons — and the demons, he decided, were the Manchus. That is what makes the Taiping unique among Chinese rebellions: not a peasant revolt swapping one dynasty for another inside the Confucian frame, but a heterodox monotheistic movement out to destroy the frame entirely. Drawing on exactly the squeezed marginal population the dynasty had created, it seizes a third of China's richest territory and rules a radical theocratic state from Nanjing for a decade. What stops it is partly the Qing and substantially the Taiping's own paranoid self-destruction — but the way the dynasty survives matters more than its survival, because it wins only by handing real military and fiscal power to Han Chinese provincial officials and their personal armies, breaking the Manchu monopoly on force forever.

bridge: While the Taiping war of Chapter 8 was bleeding China by the tens of millions, the dynasty was saved only by handing real military power to Han provincial officials and their private armies — the Manchu monopoly on force broken for good. And the foreign powers, far from waiting, came back for more in the middle of that life-or-death struggle. This chapter is the convergence of the two threats from the worst possible angle: a second foreign war landing on a dynasty already fighting for its survival at home, and the recovery that improbably follows.
setup: On a flimsy pretext in 1856, Britain and France launch the Second Opium War and march an army all the way to Beijing. The emperor flees, and the invaders do the thing that lodges in Chinese memory more than any treaty clause: they loot and burn the Yuanmingyuan, the matchless imperial garden-palace of Chapter 4, a wound the modern Chinese state deliberately keeps open. The settlement opens more ports, legalizes opium and missionary work, and — without firing a shot — lets Russia annex a chunk of Qing territory larger than France and Germany combined. Out of this nadir, though, comes a partial recovery and the figure who will dominate the rest of the dynasty: a low-born concubine who seizes power in a palace coup and rules through three child-emperors for nearly half a century. Her reputation is a minefield, and the chapter is careful to say so.

bridge: Chapter 9 left the dynasty steadied after its worst decade — the Taiping crushed, a second foreign war absorbed, the Yuanmingyuan in ashes, and Russia having sliced off a French-and-German-sized chunk of the north. The men who actually saved the throne were the Han provincial officials with Western-armed regional armies, and they drew the obvious lesson from being shelled by gunboats and rescued by Western rifles: China needed Western military technology, fast. The dynasty had stabilized. Whether stabilizing was the same as surviving is the question this chapter exists to answer.
setup: The program they launch from the 1860s is the Self-Strengthening Movement, and it is the great "what if" of modern Chinese history. For three decades genuinely capable men — Li Hongzhang above all — build arsenals, shipyards, telegraphs, coal mines, a modern fleet, and send boys to study in America, in the very same years Japan is modernizing next door. That parallel is the whole point and the comparison the entire book has been building toward: Japan tore down its old order and rebuilt the state on Western lines from the ground up; China tried to bolt Western hardware onto an unreformed Confucian society, under the slogan "Chinese learning as the base, Western learning for use." The Self-Strengtheners believed you could buy the gun without changing the society that fired it. There is a warning shot along the way, a lost war with France, and the court answers it by spending the navy's money on a marble pleasure-boat. The real exam is ten years off, and China walks toward it having learned almost nothing.

bridge: Chapter 10 set up the experiment and named the stakes: for thirty years the Self-Strengthening Movement bolted Western arsenals, shipyards, and a modern fleet onto an unreformed Confucian state, while next door Japan rebuilt itself from the ground up. China kept "Chinese learning as the base"; Japan threw the base out. The court even drained the navy's funds to build Cixi a marble boat. The whole book has been building to the moment these two answers are tested against each other in the open. That test arrives now, and it settles the argument in front of the world.
setup: In 1894 China and Japan go to war over Korea, and almost everyone expects the vastly larger China — with its famous, expensive modern fleet — to win. China is annihilated in months: the Beiyang Fleet, starved of shells by the diverted funds of the last chapter, is wrecked and then trapped and destroyed at its own anchorage. The shock is unlike any before, because China has now been crushed not by the distant West but by an Asian neighbor it regarded for two thousand years as a student of Chinese civilization, using the very model China refused to adopt. The punishing treaty hands Taiwan to Japan and triggers a scramble in which the powers carve out spheres of influence and openly discuss partitioning China the way Africa had just been carved up. The disaster breaks something loose intellectually — a reformer persuades the young emperor to attempt a wholesale transformation of the order itself, in a hundred frantic days.

bridge: Chapter 11 was the catastrophe that settled everything: defeat by Japan in 1894 shattered China's confidence, the powers began carving the country into spheres and openly discussing partition, and the young emperor's hundred-day attempt at wholesale reform was crushed by Cixi's counter-coup, the reformers beheaded or driven abroad. The lesson a younger generation drew was that the dynasty could not be fixed, only removed. Out of that wreckage — lost war, foreign scramble, failed reform, and now a savage northern drought — rises the strangest and most self-destructive episode of the whole fall.
setup: Village militias spread across the parched north practicing rituals their adherents believe make them invulnerable to bullets; Westerners call them the Boxers. Their grievances are concrete — foreign railways disturbing graves, missionary enclaves claiming legal privilege — and their program is apocalyptic: kill the foreigners and the Chinese Christians and the disasters will lift. Then the court makes the single worst decision in its history, backing the Boxers and effectively declaring war on all the foreign powers at once while the legations in Beijing are besieged. It is recognized as insane at the time — the dynasty's most powerful provincial governors simply refuse to obey and sit the war out, the clearest measure of how little central authority is left. The reckoning is total, the indemnity crushing, and the final irony is that the court then enacts the very reforms it had just killed people for proposing, including abolishing the thirteen-century-old examinations that bound the elite to the throne.

bridge: Chapter 12 ended with the dynasty hollowed from within by its own last reforms: after the Boxer catastrophe and the crushing Boxer Protocol, Cixi's court built modern schools and a modern army and, in 1905, abolished the thirteen-century-old examination system — cutting the last cord tying the educated class to the throne. Many of the brightest went to study in Japan and came back revolutionaries. Then in 1908 the imprisoned Guangxu Emperor died and, one day later, Cixi died — the timing so suspicious that a 2008 forensic test found a fatal dose of arsenic in his remains, making deliberate poisoning the strongly supported conclusion. The throne passed to a two-year-old. This is the end.
setup: The last emperor of China is a toddler, Puyi, presiding over a court out of competence, money, time, and consent. The very reforms of the last chapter created the constituencies that will bury the dynasty — a nationalist, Japan-educated officer corps with no loyalty to the Manchus, and provincial assemblies insulted to find the court's promised cabinet packed with Manchu princes. Revolutionaries abroad, led by Sun Yat-sen, have launched failed uprising after failed uprising. The revolution, when it finally comes, comes by accident: a railway dispute pulls troops out of Wuhan, an accidental bomb explosion forces a revolutionary garrison to rise early, and then province after province simply declares independence and abandons the Qing. The court turns to the one man with a loyal modern army — and he intends to take the country for himself. What ends here is not just a dynasty but the entire two-thousand-year institution of imperial monarchy, and the chapter weighs what it left behind: the map, the grievance, and the unanswered question.
